questions.question: One section of a circle graph takes up exactly one quarter of the circle. What percent of the whole does that section show?
questions.explain: A circle graph is always 100% in total, so one quarter is 100% ÷ 4 = 25%. A common trap is reading the 4 in 'one quarter' as 4%, or giving 75%, which is the part of the circle that is left over.

questions.question: A circle graph has four sections. Three of them are 35%, 20%, and 15%. What percent is the fourth section?
questions.explain: All sections of a circle graph must add to 100%, so 35% + 20% + 15% = 70%, and the missing section is 100% − 70% = 30%. The usual mistake is stopping at 70% — that is the part already used, not the piece still missing.

questions.question: A circle graph shows 60 shells collected on a beach. The 'clam shell' section is 50% of the graph. How many clam shells were collected?
questions.explain: A percent of a circle graph is a part of the total, so 50% of 60 = 60 ÷ 2 = 30 shells. Watch out for copying the number 50 straight from the graph — 50 is a percent, not a count of shells.

questions.question: A section of a circle graph has a central angle of 90°. What percent of the whole circle graph is this section?
questions.explain: A full circle is 360°, so the section is 90 ÷ 360 = 1/4 = 25%. The most common trap is treating the 90 in 90° as 90% — degrees go up to 360, but percents only go up to 100.

questions.question: In a Grade 7 tidepool study, a circle graph of 120 creatures shows barnacles at 40%. How many barnacles were counted?
questions.explain: Change the percent to a decimal and multiply: 0.40 × 120 = 48 barnacles. Two common traps are writing 40 (that is the percent, not the count) and dividing 120 ÷ 40 = 3 instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Maya is drawing a circle graph of the 40 items in her recycling bin. Exactly 10 of the items are glass. What central angle should she use for the glass section?
questions.explain: Find the fraction first, then take that fraction of 360°: 10/40 = 1/4, and 1/4 × 360° = 90°. A common trap is using the percent (25) as the number of degrees, or using 10% of 360° = 36° because the count was 10.

questions.question: A circle graph shows the after-school activity chosen by 200 students in Kelowna: soccer 25%, dance 20%, coding 15%, band 10%, other 30%. How many MORE students chose soccer than band?
questions.explain: Turn each percent into a number of students first: 25% of 200 = 50 and 10% of 200 = 20, so 50 − 20 = 30 more students. The common trap is subtracting the percents (25% − 10% = 15) and writing 15 students — a percent difference is not a number of students.

questions.question: Two schools each made a circle graph of hot-lunch orders. At Cedar School, 400 students ordered, and 30% chose salmon. At Maple School, 600 students ordered, and 25% chose salmon. Which statement is true?
options: Cedar School, because 30% is greater than 25%.
Both schools are equal, because both circle graphs are the same size.
Maple School, because 150 students is more than 120 students.
questions.explain: Percents from two circle graphs can only be compared after you turn them into quantities: 30% of 400 = 120, but 25% of 600 = 150, so Maple School had more. The biggest misconception here is that a larger percent always means a larger amount — it only does when both graphs represent the same total.

questions.question: Sofia surveyed 250 students in Burnaby about how they travel to school and made a circle graph: bus 36%, walk 24%, car 22%, and bike (the rest). How many students bike to school?
questions.explain: First find the missing percent, 100% − (36 + 24 + 22) = 18%, then take that percent of the total: 0.18 × 250 = 45 students. The common trap is answering 18 — that is the percent of the circle, not the number of students.

questions.question: A circle graph of the animals counted in a Tofino tidepool shows that the sea star section is 12% of the whole graph. The class counted 18 sea stars. How many animals were counted in total?
questions.explain: Here the part is known and the whole is missing, so divide: 18 ÷ 0.12 = 150 animals (check: 12% of 150 = 18). The common trap is multiplying 18 × 12 = 216, which happens when you use the percent-of-a-total rule backwards.

questions.question: Léa picked 60 berries near Prince George and made a circle graph. The blueberry section has a central angle of 120°. How many of the berries were blueberries?
questions.explain: Change the angle to a fraction of the circle, then take that fraction of the total: 120° ÷ 360° = 1/3, and 1/3 of 60 = 20 blueberries. Common traps are treating 120° as half the circle (30 berries) or finding the other 240° section (40 berries) instead of the blueberry one.

questions.question: At a community feast in Bella Coola, Talia fills a plate with 300 g of food and wants to show it as a circle graph. Exactly 45 g of the food is berries. What percent of the circle graph should the berry section be?
questions.explain: Compare the part to the whole: 45 ÷ 300 = 0.15, and 0.15 becomes 15%. The usual trap is grabbing the gram number and writing 45%, or finding the central angle (54°) and calling it a percent — degrees and percents are different scales, since the whole circle is 360° but 100%.

questions.question: A class in Nanaimo made a circle graph of favourite beach activities: tidepooling 30%, swimming 25%, kite-flying 20%, and beachcombing is the rest. What central angle should the beachcombing section have?
questions.explain: First find the missing percent: 100% − 30% − 25% − 20% = 25%. Then turn it into an angle out of the whole circle: 25% of 360° = 90°. Two common traps are using the 75% that was already listed instead of the leftover 25%, and writing 25° by treating the percent number as degrees.

questions.question: Jayden gets $40 a month and drew a circle graph of how he uses it: snacks 25%, bus fare 35%, savings 30%, gifts 10%. How much money do the bus fare and savings sections represent altogether?
questions.explain: Add the two sections first (35% + 30% = 65%), then take 65% of the total: 0.65 × $40 = $26.00. Common traps are stopping after one section (the $12.00 from savings alone) or slipping a decimal place and getting $2.60.

questions.question: On a Tofino field trip, Priya counted 50 tidepool creatures: 20 mussels, 15 crabs, 10 snails, and 5 anemones. She makes a circle graph of her data. Which statement about her circle graph is true?
options: The crab section is exactly one quarter of the circle.
The mussel section takes up 20% of the circle.
The mussel section takes up 40% of the circle.
The snail and anemone sections together fill half the circle.
questions.explain: Turn each count into a proportion of the 50 creatures: mussels are 20 ÷ 50 = 40%, crabs are 15 ÷ 50 = 30% (not one quarter), and snails plus anemones are 15 ÷ 50 = 30% (not half). The most common trap is using the raw count as the percent, which is where the 20% for mussels comes from.
